Chapter 1: Rethinking the Boundaries of Compassion
Most of us grow up with a pretty simple idea of what kindness means. Don’t hurt others, help out when you can, and always try to be fair. But, here’s the thing—this sense of fairness usually stops right where things start to feel unfamiliar. It’s easy to care about your neighbor’s dog, or your best friend’s cat. But that same level of concern? It rarely stretches to the animals we never actually see—the ones behind supermarket shelves or locked away in labs.
Picture this: a curious child, eyes wide with wonder, watching their family pet curl up on the living room couch. There’s this natural urge to protect, to comfort, to make sure that animal feels safe. But, just a few hours later, at dinner, that same child might eat a piece of meat without a second thought. There’s no malice in it. It’s just how things have always been. We inherit these boundaries without even realizing it.
As we grow older, the world gets a lot more complicated. News stories about animal cruelty might flash across our screens, but they’re all too easy to scroll past. The suffering of animals, especially those far away or hidden in industries we’re told are necessary—it all feels distant, almost unreal. It’s not that we don’t care. It’s just that the pain is out of sight, and the rules about who deserves our compassion rarely get questioned.
But every now and then, something breaks through. Maybe it’s a documentary showing the crowded, miserable lives of chickens in a factory farm. Maybe a friend suddenly goes vegetarian and starts opening up about why. Suddenly, those old boundaries don’t feel so solid anymore. You start to wonder: why do some lives seem to matter more than others? What makes a dog’s pain any different from a pig’s? Or a monkey’s suffering less important than a human’s?
That’s where the idea of speciesism comes in. Now, it might sound like a technical word, but at its core, it’s actually pretty simple. It’s about treating the interests of one species as more important than another’s, just because of species membership. It’s a habit so deeply woven into daily life, we barely notice it. But once you put a name to it, it’s hard to ignore.
And speciesism? It’s not just about what you eat or how you act. It’s about the stories we’ve all been told. For centuries, people have drawn a sharp line between humans and other animals, arguing that intelligence, language, or some special trait makes us unique. But if you really look at it, those justifications start to fall apart. Intelligence varies among humans, but no one says folks with less should get less protection. Language is just a tool—not a sign of worth.
So, what really matters? It’s the capacity to suffer, and to enjoy life. Pain feels the same—whether it’s in a person or a pig. Joy, fear, and the wish to avoid harm aren’t reserved just for humans. Once you realize that, those old boundaries of compassion start to blur.
And honestly, facing these questions isn’t easy. They push us to rethink habits, traditions, and sometimes even the comfort of our favorite meals. But turning away means accepting a world where suffering gets overlooked—just because it’s convenient. The very first step toward changing that? Simply noticing where those boundaries are, and asking yourself: do they really make sense?
